titulo: Used to / Would expressing habit in the past
titulo_es: Used to and would (past habits and states)
descripcion_es: Past habits and states that no longer happen; the difference from be/get used to.
resumen: Used to + infinitive expresses past habits or states that no longer happen (equivalent to Spanish “solía” or the imperfect). Would can also be used for repeated habits, but not for states.

filas: I used to play football every Saturday.
She didn't use to like coffee.
Question: Did + subject + use to + infinitive?
Did you use to live here?

explicacion.texto: Watch the spelling: in negatives and questions, after did, we write use to (without -d), because did already carries the past. Used to only exists in the past: for the present we use usually (I usually walk to work).

filas: We would go camping every summer.
I used to have long hair.
No: I would have long hair.

items: Would is used mainly in stories and memories, and usually needs context: When I was a child, my grandmother would tell me stories.
If the action happened only once or you say how many times, use the past simple: I went to Paris three times (not used to).
Do not confuse it with be used to + -ing (be accustomed to) or get used to + -ing (become accustomed to): I'm used to getting up early.

ejemplos.frase: My father used to smoke, but he gave up years ago.
ejemplos.traduccion: Mi padre fumaba, pero lo dejó hace años.

ejemplos.frase: There used to be a cinema in this street.
ejemplos.traduccion: Antes había un cine en esta calle.

ejemplos.frase: Did you use to wear glasses?
Every evening we would sit by the fire and talk.
ejemplos.traduccion: Todas las tardes nos sentábamos junto al fuego a charlar.

ejemplos.frase: I didn't use to enjoy reading, but now I love it.
ejemplos.traduccion: Antes no me gustaba leer, pero ahora me encanta.

ejemplos.frase: She isn't used to driving on the left.
ejemplos.traduccion: No está acostumbrada a conducir por la izquierda.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I use to go to the gym on Mondays.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I usually go to the gym on Mondays.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Present “suelo” is usually; used to only exists in the past.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Did you used to live in Seville?
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Did you use to live in Seville?
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: After did we write use to, without -d.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: When I was young, I would have a dog.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: When I was young, I used to have a dog.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: With states (have, be, live) we do not use would, only used to.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of used to.
ejercicios.frase: I ___ (live) in a small village when I was a child.
respuestas: used to live
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the affirmative form in the card: used to + infinitive for a past state that no longer exists. The clue is “when I was a child”: we are talking about a finished period and a situation that lasted, not a one-off event. Live is a state verb, so the natural form is used to live, not would, which the card keeps for repeated actions.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: A past state that no longer exists: used to + infinitive.
ejercicios.traduccion: Vivía en un pueblo pequeño cuando era niño.

errores_previstos.respuesta: use to live
errores_previstos.explicacion: In the affirmative we write used to, with -d; use to only appears after did.

errores_previstos.respuesta: would live
errores_previstos.explicacion: Live is a state, and the card says would is not used with states.

errores_previstos.respuesta: used to living
errores_previstos.explicacion: Used to for past habits takes the infinitive; the -ing form belongs to be used to (be accustomed to).

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of used to.
ejercicios.frase: He ___ (not like) vegetables, but now he eats them every day.
respuestas: didn't use to like
did not use to like
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the negative in the card: didn't use to + infinitive. The clue is the contrast “but now he eats them every day”: something that did not happen before and happens now. As did already marks the past, the verb use has no -d: didn't use to like. The uncontracted form, did not use to like, is also accepted.
ejercicios.traduccion: Antes no le gustaba la verdura, pero ahora la come todos los días.

errores_previstos.respuesta: didn't used to like
errores_previstos.explicacion: After didn't we write use, without -d, because did already carries the past (although it is sometimes seen in informal writing, the standard form is use).

errores_previstos.respuesta: used not like
errores_previstos.explicacion: It mixes two forms: used not to like exists but is old-fashioned and formal, and here to is also missing.

errores_previstos.respuesta: doesn't use to like
errores_previstos.explicacion: Used to only exists in the past; with does we would be talking about the present, which is not formed like this with this meaning.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete the question with the correct form of used to.
ejercicios.frase: Where ___ (you / go) on holiday when you were young?
respuestas: did you use to go
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the question structure in the card: did + subject + use to + infinitive, here preceded by the question word where. The clue is “when you were young”, a habit from a past period. In the question the past is carried by did, which is why use has no -d: did you use to go.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Question: did + subject + use to + infinitive.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Adónde ibas de vacaciones cuando eras joven?

errores_previstos.respuesta: did you used to go
errores_previstos.explicacion: After did, use is written without -d; the past is already in did.

errores_previstos.respuesta: you used to go
errores_previstos.explicacion: The auxiliary did is missing: in questions with where you must invert with did.

errores_previstos.respuesta: used you to go
errores_previstos.explicacion: In modern English, used to does not form questions by inverting like an auxiliary; we use did.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of be.
ejercicios.frase: Don't worry, I ___ used to working at night. I've done it for years.
respuestas: am
'm
ejercicios.explicacion: The card warns you not to confuse used to with be used to + -ing, “be accustomed to”. The clue is working, in -ing, and the explanation “I've done it for years”: it is not a habit that stopped, but a present situation. That is why we need be in the present with the subject I: am, or the contraction 'm (I'm used to working).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Be used to + -ing = be accustomed to; here in the present.
ejercicios.traduccion: No te preocupes, estoy acostumbrado a trabajar de noche. Lo llevo haciendo años.

errores_previstos.respuesta: was
errores_previstos.explicacion: The sentence talks about the present (Don't worry, I've done it for years), not the past.

errores_previstos.respuesta: get
errores_previstos.explicacion: Get used to means “become accustomed to”, the process; here the current state is described, which is be used to.

errores_previstos.respuesta: have
errores_previstos.explicacion: Have does not form this expression; “be accustomed to” is be used to.

ejercicios.frase: When I was a student, I ___ have a bike.
respuestas: used to
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the table in the card that separates repeated actions and states. Have, in the sense of possess, is a state, and with states only used to is possible, never would. The clue is “When I was a student”: a situation from a past period that no longer exists. The affirmative form is used to, with -d.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Have is a state: it does not take would.
ejercicios.traduccion: Cuando era estudiante, tenía una bici.

por_opcion.would: Incorrect: would only describes repeated actions; with a state like have (possess) the card rules it out.
por_opcion.used to: Correct: used to + infinitive expresses a past state that no longer exists (I had a bike before).
por_opcion.use to: Incorrect: in the affirmative we write used to; use to only appears after did in questions and negatives.

ejercicios.frase: There ___ a bakery on the corner, but it closed last year.
respuestas: used to be
ejercicios.explicacion: The card includes the phrase there used to be (es: “antes había”). The clue is the contrast “but it closed last year”: something that existed and no longer exists. Existence is a state, so it does not take would; the only valid form is used to be.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: There used to be = there was before, but not now (es: antes había).
ejercicios.traduccion: Antes había una panadería en la esquina, pero cerró el año pasado.

por_opcion.used to be: Correct: there used to be expresses that something existed before and no longer does.
por_opcion.would be: Incorrect: would is not used with states, and there would be sounds conditional (es: “habría”).
por_opcion.was used to be: Incorrect: it mixes be used to (be accustomed to) with used to; that combination does not exist.

ejercicios.frase: I ___ to Italy four times in my twenties.
respuestas: went
ejercicios.explicacion: The card says that if you state how many times something happened, you use the past simple and not used to. The clue is “four times”: specific events are being counted, not a habit described. Used to and would express habits of indefinite duration, which are incompatible with an exact number of times. That is why the answer is went.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: If you say how many times, use the past simple.
ejercicios.traduccion: Fui a Italia cuatro veces cuando tenía veintitantos años.

por_opcion.used to go: Incorrect: used to describes a habit without counting the times; with four times we use the past simple.
por_opcion.went: Correct: past simple for specific, counted events (four times).
por_opcion.would go: Incorrect: would, like used to, expresses habitual repetition, not a specific number of occasions.

ejercicios.frase: It took me months to get used to ___ in English.
respuestas: working
ejercicios.explicacion: The card points out that get used to, “become accustomed to”, is followed by -ing. The clue is get used to: here to is a preposition, not part of an infinitive, and after a preposition the verb goes in -ing. That is why it is “get used to working”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Get used to is followed by -ing.
ejercicios.traduccion: Me costó meses acostumbrarme a trabajar en inglés.

por_opcion.work: Incorrect: this is the typical mistake of taking to as the infinitive marker; in get used to, to is a preposition.
por_opcion.working: Correct: get used to + -ing, because to works as a preposition.
por_opcion.worked: Incorrect: a participle or a past form cannot follow a preposition.

ejercicios.frase: I use to walk to work every day.
respuestas: I usually walk to work every day.
I used to walk to work every day.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that used to only exists in the past and that a present habit is expressed with usually. The sentence “I use to walk” is a calque of Spanish “suelo ir”: that form does not exist in the present affirmative. There are two valid corrections depending on what you want to say: a present habit (I usually walk) or a past one (I used to walk).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Use to does not exist in the present affirmative: for a present habit we say usually; for a past one, used to.
ejercicios.traduccion: Normalmente voy andando al trabajo todos los días. / Antes iba andando al trabajo todos los días.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I use to walk to work every day.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the sentence uncorrected: use to does not exist in the present affirmative.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I usually walking to work every day.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Usually is an adverb and needs a conjugated verb: I usually walk.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I am used to walk to work every day.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Be used to means “be accustomed to” and takes -ing; besides, it does not express a simple habit.

ejercicios.frase: She didn't used to eat meat.
respuestas: She didn't use to eat meat.
She did not use to eat meat.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the spelling note in the card: in the negative, after didn't, we write use to, without -d. The clue is the auxiliary didn't, which already contains the past; repeating it in used would mark the tense twice. The correction is “She didn't use to eat meat”, or with the full form did not.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: After didn't we write use, without -d.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She didn't used to eat meat.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the sentence uncorrected; after didn't we write use, without -d.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She didn't use to ate meat.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After use to comes the infinitive (eat), not the past.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She used not eat meat.
errores_previstos.explicacion: To is missing and it is also an old-fashioned form; the normal negative is didn't use to.

ejercicios.frase: My grandparents would live in Cuenca.
respuestas: My grandparents used to live in Cuenca.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the card: would is not used for states (be, have, live, like, know…). The clue is the verb live, which describes a situation, not an action that is repeated. That is why would is changed to used to: “My grandparents used to live in Cuenca”. With would the sentence sounds conditional (es: “vivirían”).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Live is a state: used to, not would.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My grandparents would live in Cuenca.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the sentence uncorrected: would is not used with states like live.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My grandparents use to live in Cuenca.
errores_previstos.explicacion: In the affirmative we write used to, with -d.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My grandparents were used to live in Cuenca.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Be used to means “be accustomed to” and takes -ing; it does not express a past state.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite the sentence with used to.
ejercicios.frase: I had long hair in the past, but I don't now.
respuestas: I used to have long hair.
I used to have long hair, but I don't now.
I used to have long hair, but now I don't.
ejercicios.explicacion: Used to sums up in one form what the original sentence says in two parts: something was like this in the past and is no longer so. The clue is “in the past, but I don't now”. Have is a state, so only used to is possible (not would): I used to have long hair. Repeating the tag “but I don't now” or leaving it out are both accepted, because used to already implies the change.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Used to sums up a past state that no longer exists.
ejercicios.traduccion: Antes tenía el pelo largo (pero ahora no).

errores_previstos.respuesta: I used to had long hair.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After used to comes the infinitive (have), not the past.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I would have long hair.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Would is not used with states and, besides, it would mean “I would have long hair”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I use to have long hair.
errores_previstos.explicacion: In the affirmative it is used to, with -d.

respuestas: did you use to wear glasses
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the question structure in the card: did + subject + use to + infinitive. Did opens the question, then comes the subject you, then use to and the verb wear with its complement glasses. The words given already have use without -d, which is the correct form after did.

errores_previstos.respuesta: you did use to wear glasses
errores_previstos.explicacion: In a question did goes before the subject, not after it.

errores_previstos.respuesta: did you wear use to glasses
errores_previstos.explicacion: Use to goes before the main verb: use to wear.

respuestas: my grandfather would tell us stories
ejercicios.explicacion: The card says that would + infinitive describes repeated actions in memories and stories. Telling stories is an action that was repeated, not a state, so would is valid here. The order is the normal one for an affirmative sentence: subject (my grandfather), would, verb (tell), indirect object (us) and direct object (stories).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Would + infinitive for repeated actions in a memory.

errores_previstos.respuesta: my grandfather would tell stories us
errores_previstos.explicacion: With tell, the person goes before the thing: tell us stories (or tell stories to us).

errores_previstos.respuesta: my grandfather would us tell stories
errores_previstos.explicacion: The pronoun us cannot go between would and the verb.

descripcion_larga_es: Used to + infinitive expresses past habits and states that no longer happen, and is often equivalent to the Spanish imperfect or to “solía”. Would can also be used for repeated habits in stories, but never for states. It is difficult because Spanish has no special form, because it is confused with be used to (be accustomed to) and because after did we write use to, without -d.

contexto.que_es: Used to is a verb form that only exists in the past and that, followed by an infinitive, indicates that something was usual or true before and is no longer so. Would + infinitive can replace it for repeated actions, not for states. It is different from be used to + -ing and get used to + -ing, which mean “be accustomed to” and “become accustomed to”.
contexto.por_que_importa: It is the natural way to contrast the past with the present (I used to live in a village, I used to smoke), something you do constantly when talking about your own life. Confusing used to with be used to changes the meaning: “I used to work at night” (I worked at night before) is not “I'm used to working at night” (I am accustomed to it). In written exams, the spelling use/used after did is a classic mistake.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: When describing past habits or situations that have changed, often with signals like when I was a child, years ago or but now. Would appears in memories and narratives once a context has been established. Spanish speakers tend to use the past simple or to translate “suelo” as use to in the present; for the present we use usually.
